steps.title: Organic
steps.body: Organic viticulture bans synthetic fertilisers, herbicides and most synthetic pesticides. Copper and sulphur are allowed, though copper is limited in the EU to 28 kg per hectare over 7 years. In the EU, organic wine also has lower sulphite limits: 100 mg/l for dry reds compared with 150 mg/l for conventional ones. Conversion takes three years.

steps.title: Biodynamic
steps.body: Biodynamics, based on Rudolf Steiner's 1924 lectures, goes further. The farm is treated as a self-sustaining organism. Growers use preparations, such as cow manure buried in a horn over winter, in tiny doses, and time work by a lunar and astrological calendar. Certification is by Demeter or Biodyvin. Scientific evidence for the preparations is limited, but many top producers follow it.
steps.highlight: A farm as an organism, with preparations and a calendar

steps.prompt: Match each term to its focus.
steps.explanation: Each approach has its own rules and certifiers.

steps.title: Sustainable
steps.body: Sustainable programmes look at the whole business: water and energy use, biodiversity, workers' welfare and economic viability. They allow some synthetic inputs when justified. Examples include Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, the California Certified Sustainable Winegrowing programme and France's HVE, Haute Valeur Environnementale.

steps.prompt: Which of these is allowed in organic viticulture?
steps.explanation: Copper and sulphur are allowed in organic farming, with copper limited by law.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Organic bans synthetic chemicals and lowers sulphite limits
Biodynamics adds preparations and a calendar, with limited scientific evidence
Sustainable programmes cover environment, people and economics
